body: The urn was switched off at eight because nobody wanted a second cup. Seven people on stacking chairs in a side room with one radiator on, and the man near the window has been praying for some time now; he is on his third subject and there is a fourth coming. One of the women says amen roughly every forty seconds, quietly, into her hands, in the middle of his sentences. Nobody else says anything until he finishes, and then all six of them say it together, and the sound they make is the sound of a room given permission to move. Chairs go back. Somebody checks a phone.

Two different words were used in that room and they were spelled the same. The woman was agreeing with something as it went past. Everybody else was announcing that a thing had stopped. Only one of those is a prayer.

Amen has been worn down into punctuation. It is the noise that indicates a prayer has finished, said by everyone present, meaning approximately nothing, and functioning in practice as a full stop that has been said out loud.

It began as something considerably stronger, and the root is worth taking literally because the English has never been very good. The Hebrew root is about firmness — a thing being solid, reliable, load-bearing, able to be leant on. It is the same family of sounds that gives the words for faithfulness and for trust, which is not a coincidence but a definition: to have faith in something is to treat it as firm. So amen does not really mean so be it, which is a wish and costs nothing. It is nearer to that stands, or that will hold. The word is not a request at all. It is a verdict delivered by the person listening, about somebody else’s words, and it says: yes, that one is solid.

That understanding is why the older assemblies said it aloud rather than thought it, and why one station on this band is named after it. HM 303.10 Yes and Amen sits in The Crossing, the block from HM 300 to HM 320, and it is on air now, carrying covenant worship.

There is one passage that settles the matter, and it is not a comfortable one. In Deuteronomy the law is read out to the whole people from two hillsides, curse by curse, and after each one the people are instructed to say amen. Not the priest. The people. They are not agreeing that the reading was nicely done. They are putting their names to the terms, including the terms that fall on them, out loud, in front of everybody, one at a time. Amen is not a full stop. It is a signature, and it commits the person who says it. That passage is in the text specifically so that nobody can later claim they had not consented.

It is not hard to see why the word wore down, because agreement itself has become the cheapest thing we do. We are trained from about the age of ten to affirm things we have not read. The box is ticked. The terms are accepted. The message is acknowledged with a small coloured symbol meaning somewhere between yes and I have seen this. None of it binds anybody, all of it is called agreement, and after twenty years the muscle that distinguishes a real assent from a courtesy has gone slack. A person who signs forty things a week without reading one will not hear a signature in a word said at the end of a prayer.

Which puts an awkward light on ordinary church practice. Saying amen after somebody else’s prayer is a small commitment rather than a politeness. You have just signed. If you were not listening, or would not have prayed that, or would have prayed the opposite, you have signed anyway — and everybody in the room doing it at the same moment does not dilute it, any more than a document is less binding for having several names on it. This is why the response was made aloud and congregational in the first place. It was not a cue. It was the point at which the prayer stopped belonging to the man who prayed it.
There is another word doing the same work, and it is even shorter.

The obvious objection is that interior agreement ought to be enough, and it is a serious one. God is not deaf to what a person thinks, and a great deal of the most honest praying anybody does is silent and would be ruined by an audience. Nobody should be made to perform assent, and there is a long tradition of religious noise that is exactly that. So the private yes is real. What it cannot do is be witnessed. A promise nobody heard is a promise nobody can hold you to, and a person who has never said a thing out loud in front of another human being always retains the option of quietly having meant something slightly different. The spoken amen closes that door.
A word you can take back is not an agreement. It is a preference.

A woman is sitting beside a hospital bed at some hour that has stopped having a name. Her husband has been unconscious since the Thursday. The chaplain has been out in the corridor for a while talking to a nurse, and now comes in and asks whether she would like him to pray, and she says yes because it is easier than the conversation about not. He prays briefly and reasonably and without any particular skill, and near the end he says the ordinary thing about God’s will being done. She hears herself say amen. Then she sits very still, because she has spent fifty-one years saying that word at the ends of prayers and has just noticed, at ten past four in the morning, that she has put her name to something and does not know what it is.
That is the word working correctly, possibly for the first time in her life. It committed her, and she felt it commit her, and she could not get it back.

It has to be said plainly that this makes amen frightening, and the fright is not an overreaction. If the word is a signature then most of the ones you have signed were not read. Decades of prayer meetings, weddings, funerals, meals and services in which you assented, out loud, to things you had not attended to at all — that is a real reckoning and there is no comfortable way round it. It is also perfectly possible to draw the wrong conclusion and stop saying it.

That would be the wrong conclusion, and here is why. The alternative to a risky yes is not a safe yes. It is no yes at all. A person who will only agree to what he has fully understood and fully wanted will never agree to anything a covenant contains, because the nature of a covenant is that it commits you to terms you have not seen yet. The right response to noticing that the word binds is not to withdraw it. It is to start listening to what is being prayed before it reaches the end — which is what the woman with her hands over her face was doing, forty seconds at a time, all the way through.

The yes is the other half of it. Paul writes that in Christ all the promises of God are Yes, and that through him we say the Amen — God’s yes coming first, and the answering agreement going back. Two of the shortest words available in any language, doing the work of a signature on both sides of the same page. Which is also why a station named after them is not named after a slogan. It is named after the two smallest things anybody in this arrangement actually has to say.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

46 of the band’s 121 frequencies are on air, and the low end of the dial is where the singing lives. The Crossing runs from HM 300 to HM 320 and carries the gospel-forward music — praise and worship, ambient worship, country, Christian rap, Messianic celebration, the Caribbean and Hawaiian frequencies. Higher up, from HM 340 to HM 360, sits The Upper Room, which is the prayer block proper; the stations there are assigned, in build and not yet on air, so for spoken prayer the dial is still silent.

Go to HM 303.10, Yes and Amen. It is on air, it sits in The Crossing, and it carries covenant worship, which is the exact material this article has been arguing about — songs whose grammar is agreement rather than description. Listen for the specific thing. A covenant song is not a song about God from a safe distance; it is a song in which somebody says back to God what God has said first, which is the amen structure set to music and repeated until it is in the body. Sing along in a car and you will do accidentally what the Deuteronomy crowd did deliberately: put your name to terms, out loud, in a voice, before you have had time to negotiate.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download, no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive devices and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add it to your home screen if you want it closer to hand. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So here is the invitation, and it is smaller than most. Put HM 303.10 on this week while you are doing something else, and the next time a prayer is said anywhere near you — a meal, a meeting, a hospital corridor — try one experiment. Listen all the way through it, and then decide whether to say the word. Say it if you mean it and stay quiet if you do not. You will find this much harder than it sounds, and you will get it wrong within a fortnight, which is itself the most useful thing you could learn about a word you have been saying since you were four.
